 Opinion: Give back to those who sacrificed for Canada by giving blood
 Author of the article: By Special to Edmonton Journal Published Nov 09, 2026 Last updated 11 hours ago 4 minute read Join the conversation Clockwise: Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, Pte. Shaun Farrell and Pte. Aiden Goulding died while training in an exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Photo by Photo illustration Article content On Oct. 17, a grass fire swept across Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, revealing again that members of the Canadian Armed Forces are willing to suffer serious injury and to die to defend our nation. What are we willing to do in return?

Activate your Online Access Now Article content On Nov. 11, Canadians will publicly mourn Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, and Pte. Shaun Farrell, even as we remember those who died in past wars. The Books of Remembrance on Parliament Hill record more than 118,000 names of Canadians who died in military service. As Prime Minister Mark Carney told the House of Commons , “This year, we will carry more names with us.”
 Article content Article content Advertisement 1 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Yet this season of remembrance also offers us an opportunity to help. Thirty-nine other soldiers were injured, 19 of them critically , according to the first reports. Four days after the fire, Premier Danielle Smith reported that some patients had burns covering 30 to 80 per cent of their bodies. Many are in Edmonton. Burn victims often need blood products to survive .

 Article content A burn which is deep and large is life-threatening . As the wounds leak fluid and protein, patients can go into shock, resulting in damage to other organs such as kidney failure. Surgeons remove dead tissue and cover the wounds with skin grafts, often over many operations. During these times, burn victims require hospitalization, are at an increased risk of infection, and must undergo regular and painful dressing changes. During and after hospitalization, they face months to years of rehabilitation to preserve or recover function.
 Article content Patients with major burn injury have major transfusion requirements : A large number of burn patients places a great demand on blood banks to have blood products available.
 Article content Advertisement 2 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Although blood donors do not choose the recipient, physicians can treat the gravely injured only if blood and blood products are available. Many other patients also need blood and blood products: for example, patients with cancer, women who hemorrhage in childbirth and teenagers hurt in motor vehicle collisions.
 Article content Two days after the Wainwright fire, Canadian Blood Services reported that bookings had quadrupled . But the agency stressed that later appointments matter, because maintaining the supply requires continuous donations.
 Article content The supply depends on very few people. The agency estimates that though one in two Canadians is eligible to give blood, only one in 76 does.
 Article content Donating is not onerous. Donors must be at least 17 years of age and weigh at least 50 kilograms (110 pounds). A two-minute quiz at blood.ca helps determine eligibility. Appointments can be booked there, through the GiveBlood app or by calling 1-888-236-6283 (1-888-2-DONATE). The whole visit requires a little more than an hour.
 Article content Albertans have a further reason to give now. Two days after the fire, Albertans voted in a provincial referendum. About three in four chose to remain in Canada . The campaign was fierce. The disagreements it exposed merit respectful dialogue but in the face of the continuing Wainwright national tragedy, now is a time for unity.

 Advertisement 2 Advertisement This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content The soldiers at Wainwright came from across the country. The four who died were from three Western provinces. Soldiers from Ontario and British Columbia lie injured in Alberta. Approximately 28 specialized civilian medical personnel with expertise in burn care from Ontario joined those in Alberta to care for the injured.
 Article content Blood, too, crosses provincial boundaries. Canadian Blood Services manages a national inventory serving every province and territory except Quebec, which has its own agency. A donation made in Alberta can help a patient in other parts of Canada.
 Article content Whatever our political, racial, religious or gender identities, we each have blood; it is in us to give. In this season of remembrance, please consider engaging in both reflection and action. The members of the Canadian Armed Forces have always been willing to give their blood to protect us. If you are eligible to donate, then please book an appointment to give blood.
 Article content Juliet Guichon and Christopher Doig are professors at the University of Calgary Cumming School of Medicine. Dr. Doig is a critical care specialist in the intensive care unit.
